item.title: Site: Exhibition by Carlos Agredano
item.description:
Recent 2025-26 Hodder Fellow Carlos Agredano showcases new work in the exhibition, Site, in the Hurley Gallery at the Lewis Arts complex.Site follows the history of the chemical industry in twentieth-century New Jersey, whose factories supplied pesticides, plastics, and munitions to American border enforcement and the United States military. Networks of industrial firms ran from Perth Amboy, Princeton, Los Alamos, Bien Hoa, to Basrah, and their inventions left behind a toxic legacy both at home and abroad. In response to the negative environmental impact caused by the chemical industry, Congress passed the Comprehensive Environmental Response, Compensation, and Liability Act (CERCLA) in 1980, creating the list of hazardous areas known as Superfund Sites. Though it is the fifth smallest state in the country, New Jersey holds more of these contaminated sites than any other state in the United States. The exhibition places these sites beside the Minimalist and Land Art of the 1960s and 70s, whose practices mirrored the same pathways. Ideas were developed in the industrial landscapes of the East Coast, then carried to the Southwest, a region treated as open, empty, and available for experimentation and extraction. It was also where the chemical and military industries sent their inventions to be tested. Site reads these two histories together, treating the Superfund as a record of the militarization that Land Art's geography left out.Opening ReceptionAn opening reception will be held on November 10 at 4:30 p.m. in the gallery.AdmissionThe exhibition is free and open to the public.Gallery HoursOn view November 10-January 16, 2027. item.title: Earth City Building Workshop
item.description:
An all-ages collaborative building project
Stop by the Creativity Labs to add something using air-dry clay and wood to Earth City, a miniature metropolis rising from a tabletop! This activity is inspired by Earth Shed, an exhibition on view at Princeton University's School of Architecture that explores the divide between the discipline of architecture and the practice of building.
After you create with us, be sure to head over to the School of Architecture to see the exhibition, on view through December 4.

item.title: Magic: The Gathering Club Meeting
item.description: Princeton Magic: The Gathering Club meets every Saturday at 7PM in JRR A98 for a night of Commander games, free draft, and good company. Whether you've never touched a Magic card or you've got a stack of decks at home, there's a place for you at the table — we've got beginner kits with ready-to-play Standard decks and members happy to walk you through your first game step by step. New this semester, we're putting extra focus on welcoming beginners: no experience, no cards, and no prior knowledge needed, just come with curiosity. Come for the free packs, stay for the friendly competition and the community. Funded by Alcohol Initiative and USG.

item.title: Do Not Sit: Exhibition by Samuel Elijah Lee and Grace Kaneshiro
item.description:
The Program in Visual Arts and Department of Art & Archaeology present a showing of works collaboratively realized by Practice of Art major Samuel Elijah Lee ‘27 and Grace Kaneshiro ’27, a visual arts minor. Artists' Statement
The works presented in Do Not Sit are a rumination on the physical, metaphorical, and theoretical human and non-human relationships between objects and bodies. This show is not about chairs. In some ways, these works are meant to interrogate the contradictions found in ordinary objects such as the chair, which on one hand represent modes of stasis and rest, but on the other, have been radically co-opted by capitalistic means, turned from an object of leisure into an apparatus of commodity. The chair is antithetical to itself. These works are concerned with exertion, exhaustion, resistance, fortitude, and stillness. We are concerned with aspects of futurity, and the cyborgian attributes of objects that inform and animate our bodies. This was an exercise in the subversive reimagination of the form in space. We are interested in challenging how the object relates to biotic and abiotic systems across spatial and temporal intervals. Within these questions, we decided that the responsibility of labor, creative input, and execution should be shared. By this philosophy, the nature of the show is entirely collaborative, from written statements, to finished works. Although the works were inspired by everyday observation, they were equally inspired by communalism, Marxist theory, surveillance, institutional critique, and dystopic society.— Sam & GraceOpening ReceptionAn opening reception will be held on November 9 at 5 p.m. in the gallery.AdmissionThe exhibition is free and open to the public.Gallery Hours & DirectionsOn view November 9-20, 2026. item.title: Fall 2026 VIS Program Info Session
item.description:
The Program in Visual Arts hosts an info session for all sophomores interested in the program minor and the Art & Archaeology Practice of Art major. Students will have the opportunity to meet current faculty, majors, and minors to ask questions about the program and application process.This is the first of two info sessions (one will be held in February); interested students need only attend one of the two sessions.Learn more about the application to the Program in Visual ArtsQuestions? Email Professor of Visual Arts Jeff Whetstone at whetstone@princeton.edu with general questions.Visual Arts Students Develop their Practice at PrincetonMary Ma, Nsebong Adah, Sam Lee Regan, Zavier Foster, and Madison Davis share their journeys through the Program in Visual Arts. Video Transcript Video Transcript: Visual Arts Students Develop their Practice at PrincetonSam Lee Regan ‘27, Art & Archaeology Practice of Art major, Indigenous Studies and Creative Writing minors: Princeton takes its art program incredibly seriously. We have like an unfettered access to incredible artists.Zavier Foster ‘26, Politics Major, Visual Arts minor: This is a place where the faculty will give you a lot, a lot of attention despite being practicing artists.Madison Davis ’26, Art & Archaeology Practice of Art major: I don't really feel as at home at any other place on campus as I do here. And I also really value the experimentation this program has allowed me to have with my art.Mary Ma ’26, Computer Science major, Visual Arts minor: I think that also really resonates with me. I think for me, I value this program because of the freedom it provides me.Nsebong E. Adah ‘26, African American Studies major, Visual Arts and African Studies minors: The freedom kind of comes with this level of rigorousness as well, which I think I appreciate a lot.Davis: It's a very self-guided program, even though you're, you know, given a lot of help from mentors or just like your professors that you're taking classes with.Regan: It kind of also depends on like if you're, you know, like a major or minor in the program or if you're just like a student on campus that's interested in like exploring art. You can be somebody who's fully dedicated into this program and is like, this is your study. I think like what Nse said about like the rigorousness of this program is kind of what you make of it.Adah: I feel like every single one of us are sitting here because art is fundamental to who we are and who we've become as people.Foster: I'm first-generation American, so my parents are Jamaican. Over time it's a, the attitude has changed, but when I was younger, like I like, it was like I couldn't be an artist even if I could draw well. So, when I applied, it was always with the mindset of like, okay, make sure like the education with the program, whatever art program I want to do, is very highly regarded.Ma: So, I'm also like first-generation American. I applied to Art School. I got in, but like I couldn't like afford it. Princeton has amazing financial aid. Most art schools do not have amazing financial aid. I was thinking about it, like should I, you know, risk the rest of my life, I guess, to like study this thing that I think I'm really passionate about? But ultimately I decided to come here. First two years at Princeton, I honestly didn't do much art because I was really like lost in terms of like what I wanted to do with my life. But then I found myself like making art just like in my dorm. I think I mostly applied to the VIS program for the resources, but then I ended up finding a lot of mentorship as well.Davis: I think what I would say to somebody coming into Princeton who's like curious about the art programs is just like embrace your liberal arts education. Like this is why you're at this school. You should be experimenting with what you want to learn.Regan: Princeton's a top-tier research university. It's meant to explore many different facets of education and learning. And that is not something that's always afforded to an art school. A lot of my practice is about research, it's about thinking and it's about like pulling things apart and trying to understand them better. And like this is the place to do that.Adah: You're learning about science, you're learning about politics, you're learning about physics or whatever within your distribution requirements, but at the end of the day, you're forming your own generalized knowledge to look at the world.Foster: I like politics. That's been an interesting like major to have while also doing art because it helps me think more about like if I want to create something didactic or something to create a message, I kind of can go through it like empirical research-based way. And I think combining that with like the experimental processes of vis has been super interesting.Davis: I applied to most schools undecided. I didn't submit any Visual Arts portfolios. I think for Princeton I said I wanted to be an astrophysics major, architecture or chemistry, which is crazy. I've taken classes in most of those things and it's still part of like my mindset. And I actually work at a lab here that runs like 3D prints and laser cutter jobs and I do training. So, like that STEM part of Princeton is still part of my life, but it's given me a better understanding of myself through this exploration that it allowed me to have.Ma: I major in computer science and my minor is Visual Arts. There are through lines in a lot of the things that I study, but they're all, it's like very independently contained. VIS has given me a space where I can just activate like a completely different part of my brain than what I usually study, and I enjoy it that way.Adah: That's interesting because I feel like for me, my practice is so intertwined with my major. So, I'm majoring in African American Studies, getting minor in Visual Arts and a minor in African Studies. I am creating a Visual Arts thesis that's going hand in hand with my written thesis in African American Studies.Davis: It's beautiful that like both of your ways of like making art and like doing your major can exist within the same place. Like that's not the case for like most liberal arts schools or like even like fine arts schools.Adah: I agree, because even there's professors that are in multiple departments in the VIS department. Like I think I've had two or three professors that are in African American Studies and Visual Arts.Regan: Nse, Zavier and I were both in this course. It was called The Chromapolitics of Color. We went to the Guggenheim Museum and went through this exhibit that was like really incredible. And the curator had said, you know, this exhibit is inspired by the work of your professor, Tina Campt. Like this whole, this whole, and it was the entire Guggenheim. It was a moment of realization for me when I was like, oh, like yeah, if I want to be an artist, like I'm probably in the place that I actually want to be. Like the access I have here is really incredible. I think Deana Lawson's another example of this when I was like, oh my God, like I can go literally sit down and talk with Deana Lawson, who's, you know, a huge inspiration in my own work, and she will give me like her honest, thoughtful feedback.Davis: Probably the two faculty members that I'm closest with are Martha Friedman, who's been my advisor for my senior thesis, and then Daniel Heyman. I knew that the path of the artist is a crooked one, but I didn't necessarily understand like the technicalities of it. But talking to Martha and Daniel about what they've been through, like between like grad school and like undergrad and like what they've done and like how they are super successful now has made me feel more confident about myself and my work and where I'm going to be after this.Foster: This is a big part of their lives to come here and influence us and teach us and like give us access to them. And so that also taught me to like try to give access to other people as well. To younger people who might not have access to the program.Adah: All the professors in this department are willing to do that, willing to give you their time. Like it's very hard as a student when you're making student work to feel like your work is important. But I feel like they are always very encouraging and very willing to visit and very willing to say the truth about your work.Davis: The art program at Princeton functions more like what I've heard about grad programs is just super interesting. Like you're given this like very individual mentorship, you're given this stipend, you're given this space to make work, whether it be in the studio or in the gallery.Regan: In terms of undergraduate programs, I think this maybe goes the furthest. Like I kind of come back to like our faculty because the faculty are like really incredible and they're certainly at an MFA level. But as a junior, you know, I have like a really large studio and I have a computer and I have, you know, like I have been kind of given what I need to succeed. The fourth floor is where my studio is currently located. It's a group environment where it's meant to like be a part of your peers' conversations and looking at each other's work. And there is a criticality to the program in the way that students are asked to kind of interact with each other.Adah: But then senior year, you've kind of settled into what your practice is and then you're sent on to your own individual studios, which are usually shared with other people. So, you're still seeing other people's work at the same time, but it is a little bit more secluded. You get to spend more time there and you're working towards your senior show at the end of the semester.Davis: It's really amazing to have that time to make a body of work over months that you would then exhibit and have a critique about. That's not something you usually get in a undergraduate art program.Adah: There's so many resources at this school. We each get budgets our junior and senior year, basically give you the money to be able to obtain materials if they don't exist here.Foster: The materials are a really big part. Especially having the resources to even use like software like Adobe or have access to paint and pastels. Stuff that back home costs just hundreds and hundreds of dollars, probably would never be able to experiment with it.Regan: Incredible dark rooms.Davis: Incredible printmaking rooms.Adah: Full-size sculpture studio.Davis: With amazing tools for both metal and wood and eventually glass.Foster: Film editing rooms.Regan: 16 millimeter cameras.Adah: Multiple drawing and painting rooms.Regan: Plasma torch and welding, and there is a forge.Adah: Stuff is constantly being added to.Regan: The program kind of encourages you to be a multidisciplinary artist. Like they want you to explore, you know, foundational understandings at the very least, but like you can push beyond all of that and you can begin to like merge them. And I think they encourage that too. Like I'm making a lot of sculpture right now, but I'm also a photographer and I'm like wrestling with like, how do I integrate these photos into my sculpture?Ma: It's just crazy that you get the freedom and funding to like really run with the wind with whatever idea that you have.Adah: Princeton is a research institution that's focused on investing in its undergraduate students in the first place. LCA gives out summer funding awards to, I believe, from your freshman year up until your senior year, every single summer.Davis: Going into my junior year, I did a program that went to Venice and I did some printmaking stuff there and VIS gave me the Sam Hutton fund, I believe, for materials. And then with some other funding, everything was covered, I didn't have to pay anything out of my own pocket, which is great.Adah: I received the Mallach Senior Fund. And yeah, it was $5,000 and I was in South Africa for two months. And same with Madison, I didn't have to pay anything out of my own pocket.Davis: Having access to New York and the galleries and the museums probably influenced my choice to join the VIS program too, just more subconsciously.Adah: Philly is as close as people say that New York is. And there are a lot of maybe smaller institutions that are supporting interesting artists and supporting definitely earlier career artists as well.Regan: I'm planning on going to get my MFA degree directly after, I'm a non-traditional student. I'm in my 30s and so I, like I've experienced some of the life that often MFA program kind of asks you to, you know, indulge in before you go back to school. So, that's my current plan and I have some time to build a really substantial portfolio here.Ma: I'm going to be working for a tech startup in New York. I think like I still want to make art post-grad just because that's how I naturally operate.Adah: Concrete plans don't exist in this moment. I'm very much committed to a future in the arts and I don't think it would've been possible without getting into this program, to be honest.
AdmissionThe info session is free and open to all Princeton students. No registration required.DirectionsGet directions to Room 219 at 185 Nassau Street on the Princeton campusAccessibility

item.title: IHUM Open House
item.description:
The Interdisciplinary Doctoral Program in the Humanities (IHUM) invites you to our annual Open House, where you can meet IHUM students and faculty, learn about the program’s history and structure, and get a taste of our course offerings, reading groups, and public-facing salons.
Food and drink will be served. Ask us questions and meet scholars from humanistic fields across the University.
For questions regarding eligibility please refer to the IHUM website.
Open to all interested graduate students.
